topic: diagnosing failed grafts on young fruit trees in a small orchard

provenance.author: glowny-en-e
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a closed arithmetic tally of a graft order (rows, wax, labels, trays, timings) with one closed task question per turn, base is a diagnosis of unions that dried out. Grounded external referent: the box in the shed that holds the fresh grafts, named in turn 0 and again immediately before every insertion, and it stays one of the two suspects to the end.

a: Work through the graft list for the young orchard, taking the five rows one at a time.
Row one carries twenty grafts and row two carries twelve grafts of the same stock.
Row three carries nine grafts, while row four carries fifteen on the plan drawn last week.
Row five is the shortest of the five, with six grafts at the far end.
Rank the rows by graft count, largest first, and state the subtotal reached at each step.
What is the total count once all five rows have been added together?
base: Half the grafts we put onto the young apple trees last spring failed to take at all.
We cut scion wood in January and keep it wrapped in the shed until the middle of March.
The fresh grafts then stand in the box against the north wall for roughly four weeks.
The box holds forty pots, so the last dozen always end up on the floor beside it.
Those pots on the floor are the ones that fail most often, year after year.
Where would you start looking for the reason so many of the unions dried out?

a: Ranked by graft count the order runs row one, row four, row two, row three, row five.
The subtotals after each row are twenty, then thirty-five, then forty-seven grafts on the sheet.
The last two subtotals are fifty-six and then sixty-two grafts across the whole young orchard.
At two ties for every graft the order needs one hundred twenty-four ties in all.
Does the total of sixty-two grafts match the number written on the order sheet?
base: The box is the first thing I would check, because a warm corner dries a union fast.
Callus tissue wants steady warmth and damp air, and a bare wall corner gives neither.
Pots left on the cold floor stall for weeks, and the wax cracks well before they move.
A reading taken at pot level in the box tells you more than the one by the door.
Do you take any reading at all while the grafts stand there for those four weeks?

a: Now work out the wax needed, at eight grams for every graft in the order.
Give the wax weight for all five rows in the order you ranked them.
Labels go out at one per graft, plus two spare labels for each row.
Put rows one, two and three on bench one, and the other two rows on bench two.
Which wax weight belongs to row four at that fixed rate per graft?
base: We take no reading at all, and nobody has ever put a thermometer near the box.
The box sits under the window and it has been in that spot for six seasons.
We wrap each union in tape and brush wax over the top of the cut.
By the end of March the shed swings from four degrees at night to twenty by noon.
Would moving the last dozen pots into the box be enough on its own?

a: Row one takes one hundred sixty grams of wax, and row four takes one hundred twenty grams.
Row two takes ninety-six grams, and row three takes seventy-two grams of wax.
Row five takes forty-eight grams, which is the smallest amount on the whole sheet.
Bench one needs forty-seven labels for its three rows, counting the spares you asked for.
Does the wax total of four hundred ninety-six grams agree with the store list?
base: Moving them in would help, though a box under a window can cook the grafts by noon.
What you want is a steady fifteen degrees, not the brightest spot in the whole shed.
I would shift the box away from the glass and cover the pots with a light cloth.
Tape and wax matter less than the cut itself, which has to meet bark to bark.
How long does one union take you from the first cut to the finished wrap?

a: One correction before we go on: row three carries eleven grafts and not nine.
Redo its wax and its labels, and leave the other four rows exactly as they stand.
Then give the new totals for grafts and for wax across the whole order.
After that list the five rows in the order the crew will work them tomorrow.
Which row comes first under the order row two, row five, row one, row four, row three?
base: A union takes me about two minutes, and the knife gets a fresh edge every morning.
The scion wood comes off the old trees on the far side of the field.
Nobody has changed that habit in years, and the box has stood in the same place just as long.
The sticks look sound, but the bark slips on some of them by the end of March.
Could the way we hold that wood cost us half a season of growth?

a: Row three at eleven grafts now takes eighty-eight grams of wax and thirteen labels in total.
The new graft total is sixty-four across the five rows of the young orchard.
The new wax total comes to five hundred twelve grams for the whole order.
Bench one now needs forty-nine labels in all, while bench two still needs twenty-five.
Does the working order still open with row two as it was set out?
base: Slipping bark means the wood woke early, and a stick in leaf will never make a union.
Cold and dark keeps it dormant, so a shed in March is far too mild for it.
I would move the bundle to the cellar and check the buds once a fortnight.
Then graft the whole batch in one week rather than spreading it over three.
Do you still have any sticks left from the bundle you cut this January?

a: Turn the whole order into trays of pots, at twelve pots to the tray.
Tell me how many full trays that needs and how many pots are left over.
Then split the wax total into two tins of equal weight, and give each figure.
The bench opens at eight in the morning, with a row finished every forty minutes.
How many full trays does a count of sixty-four pots come to?
base: There are maybe thirty sticks left in the shed, wrapped in the same damp sacking.
We could graft two batches on the same day if the bench is clear by noon.
The box holds forty pots, though, and the first batch already fills most of the shelf.
Standing two batches side by side would mean stacking pots, and stacked pots dry out faster.
Would a stacked pot spoil the comparison we are trying to set up here?

a: Sixty-four pots make five full trays with four pots left standing over.
Each of the two tins holds two hundred fifty-six grams of wax for the day.
Row two starts at eight, and row five follows it at eight forty.
Row one begins at nine twenty and row four begins at ten in the morning.
Row three closes the bench at ten forty, ending a run of three hours twenty.
base: Stacking would spoil it, because the pots underneath stay damp while the top ones dry.
Set both batches on one shelf and swap their ends halfway through the four weeks.
Better still, cut each batch in half so the whole trial fits on that shelf.
Graft, wrap and label them within the same hour so nothing else differs between them.
Write the temperature at pot level on the label every morning without fail.

a: Print a short list of the four steps in order for the crew tomorrow morning.
Step one is cutting, step two is fitting and step three is tying the union.
Step four is waxing, and each step needs the clock time for row two.
Cutting starts at eight in the morning and the waxing finishes at eight forty.
Which clock time closes the fitting if cutting and fitting take ten minutes each?
base: That sounds workable, and halving both batches costs us nothing but a few spare pots.
I will write the readings on the labels so whoever waters them keeps the record going.
One worry is the quince stock, which breaks bud a good fortnight before the apple.
If the quince runs ahead, its grafts will be swelling while the apple ones sit still.
Should the quince pots go into the cellar while the apple batch settles in the box?

a: Step one is the cutting at eight, and it runs ten minutes for the whole row.
Step two is the fitting from eight ten until eight twenty as you set it out.
Step three is the tying between eight twenty and eight thirty on the same bench.
Step four is the waxing from eight thirty until eight forty, closing that row.
Row five follows at eight forty, and that order holds for the whole morning.
base: Yes, hold the quince pots in the cellar for the fortnight the apple stock needs.
Cold holds them back just enough that both batches break at about the same time.
Bring them up a few days before the buds move so the roots wake first.
Then they go onto the shelf with the rest and the labels pick up the readings.
Two seasons of that and the failures should explain themselves from the notes alone.
